title: How Aptitude Assessments Work
relevance: Campus and early SDE OAs filter on timed aptitude and quant MCQs where pattern recognition, mental agility, and speed matter more than deep theory.
company_notes: Product-SDE OAs (Microsoft, Google, Uber): mostly DSA plus 10–15 logical/quant MCQs (combinatorics, probability, bitwise) at 1–2 mins/MCQ beside 45+ min coding. Service-firm OAs (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture): quant, logical, verbal, DI at 45–60 secs/question. Quant/prop-trading (De Shaw, Millennium, Jane St): advanced probability, EV, stats, mental math, game theory, brain teasers under brutal timed or live pressure. BA/analyst: statistics, guesstimates, DI, case reasoning.

phases.goal: Establish what aptitude screens measure and how formats differ by hiring track.

must_hit.point: Aptitude is not a test of deep theoretical mathematics; it tests pattern-recognition, mental agility, and speed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the three skills tested and explicitly rejects deep-theory framing.

must_hit.point: Product-SDE OAs (Microsoft, Google, Uber) are mostly DSA coding with 10–15 logical or quant MCQs on combinatorics, probability, and bitwise logic, timed at 1–2 mins/MCQ alongside 45+ min coding; service-firm OAs (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture) cover quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal ability, and DI at 45–60 secs/question; quant/prop-trading (De Shaw, Millennium, Jane St) emphasize advanced probability, expected value, statistics, mental math, game theory, and brain teasers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three tracks with matching format/focus and the timing figures from the landscape table.

must_hit.point: Match prep to the target track: Google-style focus on bitwise tricks and probability; Jane Street on live mental math and expected value; TCS NQT on speed across all standard arithmetic topics.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the three target-to-prep pairings from the keypoint, not a one-size-fits-all plan.

probes: What do aptitude assessments actually measure, and how do Product-SDE, service-firm, and quant/prop-trading OAs differ in format and timing?
If you were targeting Google versus Jane Street versus the TCS NQT, how would your prep emphasis change?

hints.1: Start from why companies run these tests, then contrast hiring tracks.
hints.2: Separate Product-SDE (DSA + short quant/logic MCQs), service-firm (full aptitude sections, speed-heavy), and quant/prop (advanced probability/EV/mental math), then map prep to each.
hints.3: Aptitude = pattern-recognition, agility, speed—not deep theory; Product-SDE: DSA + 10–15 MCQs at 1–2 mins with 45+ min coding; service firms: quant/logical/verbal/DI at 45–60 secs; quant shops: EV/mental math under brutal limits; prep Google→bitwise/probability, Jane Street→mental math/EV, TCS NQT→speed across arithmetic.

phases.goal: Show the memorized tables, divisibility/cyclicity rules, and multiplication tricks that cut seconds under time pressure.

must_hit.point: Memorize essential tables before the test: fractions to percentages (e.g. 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/8 = 12.5%), squares from 1 to 30, cubes from 1 to 15, and powers of 2 up to 2^12.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four table families and cites representative fraction↔% facts rather than calculating from scratch.

must_hit.point: Divisibility rules: 2/4/8 check the last 1/2/3 digits; 3/9 require the digit sum divisible by 3 or 9; 5 needs last digit 0 or 5; 6 needs both 2 and 3; 7 doubles the last digit and subtracts from the rest; 11 needs the alternating digit sum to be 0 or divisible by 11.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites each rule in the file’s form, including the 7 and 11 procedures.

must_hit.point: Unit-digit cyclicity: ends 0, 1, 5, 6 have cycle length 1 (stay the same); 4 and 9 have cycle length 2; 2, 3, 7, 8 have cycle length 4 (e.g. 7 → 7, 9, 3, 1)—reduce the exponent mod the cycle length to pick the matching cycle entry.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Groups endings by cycle length 1/2/4 and explains remainder-to-cycle-position lookup.

must_hit.point: Fast multiplication: ×11 splits the number and inserts the digit sum in the middle; ×25 appends two zeros then divides by 4; near-base (e.g. base 100) uses deficits or surpluses against the base; split-and-add breaks a factor into a sum.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the four tricks with the ×11 / ×25 / near-base structure from the keypoint.

probes: Which tables must you memorize, and what are the divisibility rules for 8, 9, 7, and 11?
How do you find the unit digit of a large power using cyclicity, and how do the ×11, ×25, and near-base multiplication tricks work?

hints.1: Think about what you refuse to recompute under a 45–60 second clock.
hints.2: Cover fraction/%/squares/cubes/powers-of-2 tables, then divisibility, unit-digit cycles, then ×11/×25/near-base.
hints.3: Tables: 1/9=11.11%, squares to 30, cubes to 15, 2^12; 8→last 3 digits, 9→digit sum, 7→double-last subtract, 11→alternating sum; cycles 1/2/4 by ending digit; ×11 insert sum, ×25 → /4 after two zeros, near-base deficits/surpluses.

phases.goal: Choose when to compute exactly versus approximate aggressively under MCQ time pressure.

must_hit.point: When multiple-choice options are far apart, approximate aggressively—calculating the exact decimal is often a trap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the far-apart-options rule and names exact-decimal chasing as the trap.

must_hit.point: Percentage estimation builds from 10% (move the decimal once), 5% (half of 10%), and 1% (move the decimal twice), then sums the pieces needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the 10%/5%/1% decomposition rather than a full precise percent calculation.

must_hit.point: Order-of-magnitude checks catch decimal errors: e.g. 4.1 × 213 must be slightly more than 4 × 200 = 800; a result like 87 or 8000 means a missed decimal place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses a rough product bound and flags wildly smaller/larger answers as decimal mistakes.

probes: When should you stop chasing an exact decimal on an aptitude MCQ, and how do you estimate a percentage quickly?
How would you sanity-check a product like 4.1 × 213 before locking an answer?

hints.1: Ask whether the options are close enough to reward precision.
hints.2: If options are spread out, use 10%/5%/1% percentage pieces and a rough magnitude bound on products.
hints.3: Far-apart options → approximate; build % from 10, half-of-10, and 1; 4.1×213 ≈ just over 800—87 or 8000 means a decimal slip.

phases.goal: Apply story-stripping on wrapped OAs and the structured think-aloud attack on live puzzle interviews.

must_hit.point: Modern OA word problems wrap math in narrative or software context—strip the story immediately to expose the underlying model (e.g. relative speed, set theory, or bitwise arithmetic).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says strip-the-story first and names example underlying models from the keypoint.

must_hit.point: For quantitative, prop-trading, and analytical live interviews, grading is based on reasoning and structured approach, not just the final number; blurting a memorized answer hurts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts think-aloud structured reasoning with blurting a memorized final answer.

must_hit.point: The 5-step interview attack: restate the problem and constraints; simplify or try a small case; find an invariant or expected value; generalize to N; sanity-check edge cases (N=0, N=1, or probabilities of 0 or 1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all five steps in order, including the small-case and edge-case checks.

probes: You get a robot/track word problem in an OA—what do you do before computing?
Walk me through how you would attack a live probability or brain-teaser interview question out loud.

hints.1: Separate wrapped MCQs from live puzzle interviews.
hints.2: For OAs, name the hidden model after stripping story; for interviews, use the five-step think-aloud sequence.
hints.3: Strip narrative → relative speed / sets / bitwise; live rounds grade reasoning not the blurted number; steps = restate → small case → invariant/EV → generalize → sanity-check N=0/1 or prob 0/1.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: If MCQ options are far apart, approximate aggressively and skip exact decimals. Build percentages from 10%, 5%, and 1% pieces, and use order-of-magnitude product checks (e.g. 4.1×213 just over 800) to catch decimal-place errors.

tradeoffs.topic: Broad aptitude drill vs target-track prep
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Match prep to the role: Google-style Product-SDE → bitwise tricks and probability; Jane Street-style quant → live mental math and expected value; TCS NQT-style service OA → speed across all standard arithmetic topics.
In quant/prop/analytical interviews, graders score reasoning and structured approach; blurting a memorized answer hurts—restate, small-case, invariant/EV, generalize, then sanity-check.

gotchas.trap: Calculating every quantity from scratch under timed OA pressure.
gotchas.correction: Memorize fraction↔percentage, squares 1–30, cubes 1–15, and powers of 2 through 2^12, and apply divisibility, unit-digit cyclicity, and ×11/×25/near-base tricks to shave seconds.

gotchas.trap: Chasing an exact decimal when the multiple-choice options are far apart.
gotchas.correction: Approximate aggressively with 10%/5%/1% percentage pieces and order-of-magnitude checks; exact decimals are often a trap.

gotchas.trap: Solving the wrapped story instead of the underlying math model.
gotchas.correction: Strip the narrative immediately to expose relative speed, set theory, bitwise arithmetic, or similar.

gotchas.trap: Blurting a memorized puzzle answer without showing work.
gotchas.correction: Think out loud with the 5-step attack: restate constraints, try a small case, find an invariant or EV, generalize to N, then sanity-check edge cases.
